rows.summary: useState and useReducer lower to signals with React render snapshots (handlers and effects read the committed state, functional updaters the latest), Object.is bail-out, lazy initializers (inline or named), useReducer init, a stable dispatch, and React's update lanes (discrete events commit in a microtask, other updates in a later task).

Effects run in React's commit order (insertion, layout before paint, passive after paint or synchronously after discrete events; children before parents; cleanups before re-runs; parent-first unmount) with Object.is deps, and setups/cleanups read the state and props of their own commit. useMemo/useCallback honour deps synchronously. A component in one conditional branch unmounts and remounts with fresh state; one stateful component type in both branches of a ternary (or chain, or early returns) keeps its instance and switches its props. Effects without deps re-run on the component's own state/props changes only; each divergence has a KR2xxx diagnostic.
knownLimits: A same-type pair that cannot be lowered to one element (render-prop children, a differing ref or spread, a wrapper element built by each branch) restarts the component on the flip and warns with KR8360.
A stateless component or an external island in both branches is not merged: uncontrolled DOM state inside it resets on the flip.

rows.summary: Context resolves at the reader's position like React: Provider, React 19 <Ctx value>, Consumer render props, object defaults, nested and self-nesting providers, and providers around props.children; constant values fold at build time and state-driven values stay reactive. Object and callback refs (with React 19 cleanup functions), ref as a prop, forwardRef, createRef, useRef, and useImperativeHandle with deps attach before layout effects and detach on unmount.

useTransition and startTransition support async actions: isPending stays true until the action, its awaited work and overlapping transitions settle, and a transition keeps revealed Suspense content. useDeferredValue (with React 19 initialValue) catches up in a later task; useSyncExternalStore follows the store by Object.is and unsubscribes on teardown. Updates after an await are ordinary updates, as in React 19.

Lowered onto a runtime instance with React 18 ordering: batched setState with callbacks, forceUpdate, componentDidMount/DidUpdate (props and state, children first)/WillUnmount on branch removal, shouldComponentUpdate, PureComponent, getDerivedStateFromProps, getSnapshotBeforeUpdate, defaultProps, contextType, accessors, private members, and instance refs. UNSAFE_componentWillMount, legacy context and other statics are rejected with KR3xxx diagnostics.

Classes with getDerivedStateFromError/componentDidCatch catch errors from descendants' render, bindings, lifecycles and effects (not event handlers or async code), unmount the failed subtree, and recover on reset. A throw while the page is built renders the boundary fallback (KR3009). Uncaught errors unmount only the failing component. Each Preact island has its own error boundary and marks a fallback placeholder when rendering fails.
knownLimits: Build-time boundary fallback for a browser-only island subtree is client-only; the island error boundary handles the client render failure.
Island error boundaries catch Preact render errors, not event-handler or asynchronous errors.

rows.summary: 404.tsx or not-found.tsx and error.tsx or 500.tsx in any pages directory are that segment's pages. The nearest not-found page answers an unmatched URL, a closed dynamic route's unknown param and notFound() (status 404, inside the segment's layouts); the nearest error page answers an uncaught server error (status 500, sanitized message plus a digest) and, as a client error boundary around the segment's children, render, effect and reactive errors, with reset() and a hand-over to the next boundary up when an error page itself fails. The router swaps either page in place and keeps shared layouts. Pages are noindex and stay out of the sitemap and the route list.
knownLimits: A page that throws while it is prerendered still fails the build (KR3010); the segment error page is not baked in as a build-time fallback.
Segment pages are always prerendered; request-time rendering modes on them are ignored with KR9003.
In the server-rendered error page, error.message and error.digest are filled into the HTML before hydration; text derived from them at render time appears once the page hydrates.

rows.summary: Static Children helpers and cloneElement fold at build time. Lists reconcile by key with React semantics: rows keep DOM, input and focus state, component state, effects and refs across reorder, insert and removal (minimal moves), unkeyed lists match by index, items update in place, duplicate keys warn, and a changed key on a single element remounts it. Hydration adopts server-rendered rows by key. Missing, duplicate and partial keys are diagnosed (KR6001-KR6003). Refs in lists attach per item and detach when an item is removed.
knownLimits: Some dynamic Children helpers and cloneElement calls cannot be folded at build time and use the compat runtime.
List key inference is conservative for computed keys; rows without a stable key may be adopted by position.

rows.summary: React 17+ root delegation with capture then bubble order, native listener interleaving, stopPropagation, the synthetic event surface, React onChange semantics, focus/blur bubbling, per-element enter/leave, media and composition events. Unknown or lowercase event props are diagnosed (KR5001, KR5002).
knownLimits: Island event handlers run on Preact's event system, so Krate's source-level event diagnostics do not apply inside a compiled package.
Controlled pointer/focus state in a compiled package is the package's responsibility; Krate only bridges page signals and callbacks.

rows.summary: Controlled text, select (single and multiple), checkbox, radio group, textarea, number and range inputs restore to state after onChange; uncontrolled defaultValue/defaultChecked only set defaults; form reset and value={undefined} follow React. Form diagnostics: KR5004 to KR5007. React 19 form actions (action/formAction functions, reset after success) run in the browser gate. No-JS server action posts reach the server and redirect back; the returned state is carried in a short-lived flash cookie that useActionState reads on the next page, but a pre-rendered page is not re-rendered with it without script.
knownLimits: Controlled controls inside a compiled package use Preact's controlled-input behavior; Krate's form diagnostics apply to source components only.
Server action forms remain source-level; a compiled package receives the action runtime but not Krate's form lowering.

rows.summary: createPortal and Portal mount into document.body or a resolved container after hydration, follow conditional branches, unmount with their component, and bubble React events to the portal's React ancestors. Like React, portal content is not part of the server-rendered HTML.

Boundaries show their fallback while use(promise), a resource or a lazy component inside is pending, reveal siblings together with React's 300ms reveal throttle, and nest independently (innermost wins). Content that cannot resolve at build time ships the fallback and hydrates into the content. A non-transition update that suspends hides the content in place and shows the fallback; a transition keeps the revealed content. lazy() (static import or a loader resolving to a local component) shows the fallback until its separately loaded hydration chunk or loader is ready. Matches React in the browser differential suspense fixtures.

Source useActionState (queued, previous state over the action transport, permalink no-JS fallback), useFormStatus (form-scoped), useOptimistic (revert on settle), requestFormReset, and function form actions are lowered and run in the browser gate. Compiled packages get the same useActionState/useOptimistic runtime; their useFormStatus is idle. use() and async startTransition are tracked under Suspense and transitions.
knownLimits: Compiled packages get useActionState and useOptimistic through the compat runtime; useFormStatus is idle inside an island.
Use() and async transitions in compiled packages follow Preact compat behavior, not the source-component transition lowering.
React 19 action hooks run in source components; a compiled island gets the compat runtime subset (useFormStatus is idle).

rows.summary: useId gives every component instance (children, nested children, lists, repeated components, conditional branches, layouts, rows added at runtime) an id that is the same in the static HTML and the hydration code, so htmlFor and id pairs match. useEffectEvent lowers to a stable function that reads the latest props and state and does not subscribe the effect that calls it. <Activity mode> renders its children in a wrapper that hides them while keeping state, cleans their effects up while hidden and runs them again when visible. <ViewTransition> names its element child for the router's view transition support (name and default class). The experimental names (unstable_Activity, unstable_ViewTransition, unstable_useEffectEvent, SuspenseList) are accepted; props with no effect warn (KR8031).

Strings and numbers render as attributes, true as an empty attribute and false is omitted. Objects, arrays and functions render no attribute on the server and are set as properties on the client, also when the element class is defined after the page loads. Components that render such props hydrate so the property is set.

rows.area: Component tiers: client APIs, conflicts and higher-order components
rows.summary: A server, static or runtime component that uses state, effects or event handlers fails the build (KR7110) with the fix, instead of shipping a dead page. Two tier sources that disagree for one component fail (KR7115). A tier decorator on an HOC-wrapped default export classifies the component and the HOC is applied, also when it is declared in another module; an HOC that cannot be inlined fails (KR8030).

File-level "use server" modules compile to hashed POST endpoints with client proxies, bound arguments, no-JS form posts, SSR forms, registry validation, origin checks, body limits, and no-store responses. Enhanced forms return results without reloading; errors use a {message, digest} envelope; actions read headers() and cookies() and can redirect(). Exports built by a wrapper (createAction(...)) are checked when the module loads. Inline "use server" functions in server components are hoisted into generated actions, with the values they close over sealed per request (async components); in a client module they are a coded build error (KR7001).

@krate/runtime/cache provides revalidatePath, revalidateTag, unstable_cache and unstable_noStore; server fetch honors next.tags/next.revalidate/cache options; pages accept export const revalidate and export const dynamic. Revalidation is applied across the SSR renderer workers, Go region cache, QuickJS and Node API data caches before an action or API route responds; static (SSG) targets are reported as skipped (KR8603).
knownLimits: Caches are in memory per server process; multiple krate serve instances do not share them.
Static (SSG) pages cannot be revalidated at runtime; revalidatePath reports them as skipped.
Tags are recorded for data read during the page render; region renders and Go components do not record tags.

rows.summary: Radix and other compiled packages run as Preact islands with live props, callbacks, portals, controlled primitives, per-island entries bundled with shared modules, server-rendered initial markup, hydration, and an island error boundary. Known Preact limits: an uncontrolled Radix Tooltip closes right after it opens, and a layer opened inside another layer's portal content dismisses the outer layer; both have documented workarounds.
Copied shadcn source components, cva/cn folding, cards, controlled filters, and derived lists run in the browser corpus.
The benchmark Next App Router fixture is the migration-shaped corpus. It is source-corpus coverage today, not a browser-run Krate app.

Imported local React-compatible modules can be used as tags inside a compiled island and are bundled with it. Same-file Krate functions are diagnosed because they cannot cross the Krate/Preact runtime boundary.

rows.area: npm React hook libraries (zustand, react-hook-form, SWR, TanStack Query, ...)
rows.summary: A user module that calls a hook of an npm package built on React (or a store hook made by its factory, or a custom hook wrapping one) is bundled for Preact (react resolves to preact/compat, CommonJS require of react is bridged), rendered on the server and hydrated in place. The islands of all pages are bundled together with code splitting, so a store module is one store for the whole site and its state survives client-side navigation, forward and back; a leaving island unmounts and releases its subscriptions. A provider a layout wraps around its children (a query client, a Redux store, a theme) is lifted into the islands, one instance for every island of the page, with nested layouts composing; a provider that cannot be lifted is reported (KR8015, KR8016). Pages rendered per request (SSR, ISR) answer with the islands' build-time markup and hydrate. Checked by hand in Chromium against zustand 5.0.16, TanStack Query 5.105.3, react-redux 9.3.1 with Redux Toolkit 2.14.0 and styled-components 6.6.0 (ThemeProvider), and earlier against valtio 2, jotai 2, react-hook-form 7, SWR 2, TanStack Table 8, react-i18next 15 and usehooks-ts 3; the repository tests use stand-in packages with the same import shapes and behavior.
knownLimits: A layout, template or server-rendered page cannot call these hooks outside a "use client" module; the build fails with KR8013. Their components (icons, Radix primitives) render in async pages, layouts and components as client boundaries.
A layout provider whose props read the layout's params, a signal or a state setter, or that renders markup of its own, cannot reach the islands (KR8015, KR8016).
State inside a component resets when its island unmounts on navigation; module-level state is kept.
A page that is itself such an island cannot take route props (KR8013) or use Krate-only APIs in the same module.
An island in a page rendered per request is server-rendered from build-time props; a prop known only per request makes it client-only.
Only Chromium was run for the browser check.

rows.area: Compiled React packages in async pages, layouts and server components (lucide-react, Radix)
rows.summary: The components a server module imports from a package built on React are client boundaries: rendered with Preact on the server, plain HTML when they have no state or effects (an icon), a hydrating island otherwise. Parts of a compound component (Radix Dialog.Root with its Trigger and Content) stay in one Preact tree. Async layouts render per request with the page below them, so a layout can read a session and gate its subtree with redirect() or notFound(). Checked in Chromium against lucide-react 1.28 and radix-ui 1.6 (checkbox, dialog).
knownLimits: Props follow the "use client" rules: serializable values and server actions, no inline functions.
A synchronous (static) layout cannot host compiled components; make it async (KR8013).
Server components placed between the parts of a compound component render to HTML, so the parts around one do not share a tree.
Only Chromium was run for the browser check.

rows.summary: Components built with styled-components, @emotion/styled, the emotion css prop (with the jsxImportSource pragma) or MUI run as Preact islands and are styled in the browser. They are client-only because the styles are created while rendering, so the server HTML holds an empty placeholder (KR8008 notice). A css prop without emotion's runtime is reported (KR8014). A ThemeProvider in a layout reaches them. Checked by hand in Chromium against styled-components 6, @emotion/styled and @emotion/react 11 and MUI 9.
knownLimits: No server-rendered markup or styles: content appears when the island mounts.
A project-wide jsxImportSource for emotion in tsconfig is not supported; use the per-file pragma.

rows.summary: client:visible and client:idle on an island's root tag defer mounting until the island is near the viewport or the browser is idle. The server markup stays; the chunk is neither preloaded nor fetched before then, and the directive never reaches the component. client:load is the default.

A user module that imports a package built on react-reconciler (detected from its dependencies) or listed in react.islands runs in a client-rendered island bundled with real react and react-dom, with no Preact alias in its subtree. The server emits a placeholder (client:fallback text). All islands of a page mount from one entry, and the pages of a site share one React chunk that only pages with such an island load. Signal props bridge in as for other islands.
knownLimits: Client-rendered only: no server markup beyond the fallback text.
Adds react and react-dom (about 60 KB gzipped) plus the library to the pages that use it.
Layout providers are not applied; Krate components cannot be passed in as children (same-file ones are diagnosed with KR8007).
Layouts and async server pages cannot host them (KR8013).

rows.summary: A module using Canvas, useFrame and the other fiber APIs runs as a real-React island (fiber depends on react-reconciler, so it is detected without configuration). Verified by hand: Canvas with a mesh renders a WebGL scene under three 0.170 and @react-three/fiber 9.8.
knownLimits: The mechanism is tested in CI with a minimal react-reconciler renderer; the library itself was verified by hand in Chromium (@react-three/fiber 9.8, three 0.170, React 19.3) and is not installed in CI.
WebGL output is client-only; there is no server rendering.

rows.summary: drei peer-depends on @react-three/fiber, so a module importing it runs as a real-React island with no configuration. Verified by hand: OrbitControls inside a fiber Canvas under @react-three/drei 10.7.
knownLimits: The mechanism is tested in CI with a minimal react-reconciler renderer; the library itself was verified by hand in Chromium (@react-three/drei 10.7) and is not installed in CI.
Only OrbitControls was exercised; other helpers have not been tried.

rows.summary: react-konva depends on react-reconciler, so a module using Stage, Layer and the shape components runs as a real-React island with no configuration. Verified by hand: a Rect moves when island state changes under react-konva 19.3 and konva 9.3.
knownLimits: The mechanism is tested in CI with a minimal react-reconciler renderer; the library itself was verified by hand in Chromium (react-konva 19.3, konva 9.3) and is not installed in CI.
The canvas is client-only; there is no server rendering.

rows.summary: Islands with build-time-known props are server-rendered with Preact and hydrated in place. The island entries of all pages are bundled together, so modules pages share are shared files. Unknown props, browser-only components, and portals fall back to client-only with a warning. A page rendered per request (SSR, ISR, streaming) answers with the placeholders and build-time markup of its islands instead of running them in the Node renderer; request-time props for an island are not supported.
The island build warns below 10.20. The conformance jobs exercise the minimum, an intermediate version, and the workspace version.

124 source-component fixtures (React 18 corpus plus the React 19 reference app) run in real React 19 and in Krate in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit; DOM, form state, focus, and effect/lifecycle/ref ordering are compared after every step. Known divergences are tracked with a severity, and KRATE_REACT_EXIT=1 fails while P0/P1 entries remain.
knownLimits: Four P2 render-count/useId formatting differences remain documented in testdata/reactbrowser/divergences.json.

rows.summary: Fixtures for useActionState, useOptimistic, useFormStatus, form and button actions with auto-reset, use(promise) and use(context), ref as a prop, ref cleanup callbacks, async transitions, useDeferredValue initial values, document metadata, and server actions under the real server.

rows.target: Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare and Node hosting
rows.summary: krate deploy bundles the portable server handler (SSR, ISR, streaming, async server components, JS/TS API routes, server actions, middleware, redirects, rewrites, headers) into one self-contained module for --target node, vercel, netlify and cloudflare. Per-segment not-found and error pages and middleware on prerendered pages work on every target. A request matrix gives the same status, security and cache headers, redirects and bodies as krate start; Go API routes, Go components and sidecars are refused at deploy time.
knownLimits: ISR, region and data caches are per instance on serverless targets; revalidatePath/revalidateTag only reach the instance that handled the request (reported under skipped). Pass an isrStore to createKrateHandler to share the page cache.

With middleware, Vercel and Netlify send every page request to the function, which serves prerendered HTML from the bundle (bundle size grows with static pages); assets keep going to the CDN. A public file without an extension is treated as a page there.
Legacy (req, res) API handlers, Go API routes, Go components, the API sidecar and community plugin serve hooks are not supported on serverless targets.
Cloudflare bundles fail at build time for Node built-ins outside nodejs_compat (fs, vm, net, child_process).

rows.target: Next.js sitemap.ts, robots.ts, manifest.ts, opengraph-image and twitter-image
rows.summary: sitemap.ts, robots.ts and manifest.ts build sitemap.xml, robots.txt and manifest.webmanifest; opengraph-image and twitter-image files (including per-segment and per-generateStaticParams ones) build real PNGs from ImageResponse JSX with a pure Go renderer (flex layout, text and fonts, colours, gradients, images), and feed og:image and twitter:image. Anything the renderer cannot draw is a build error (KR7131). A file wins over a plugin (KR7133). Per-request ImageResponse works in Node API routes under krate start only; Workers and serverless functions have no renderer. krate migrate nextjs maps these files natively. Not supported: CSS grid, transform, filter, SVG, icon and apple-icon files, opengraph-image.alt.txt.

Code is highlighted by chroma at build time, by the same lexers in the Node renderer for request-time code, and by the same lexers loaded on demand for code that changes in the browser. The lexers are exported from the binary's own chroma and run token for token (the markup is identical), in light and dark from one stylesheet, with a size, line and time limit that leaves text plain instead of stalling.
knownLimits: Request-time highlighting runs in the Node renderer; serverless deploy targets write plain text.
The browser and request-time highlighters ship 16 languages; other languages are highlighted at build time only.
A Markdown fence that names a language outside the shipped set leaves the snippet plain.

rows.summary: The shell opens a window around the system webview (WebKitGTK 4.1 through purego on Linux, WKWebView on macOS, WebView2 on Windows) and serves the built UI from an in-process custom scheme with a content security policy. Navigation away from the app origin is blocked, paths cannot escape the asset directory, and browser mode serves the same app on a loopback port behind a session token.
knownLimits: Linux GUI tests need a display and WebKitGTK 2.40 or newer (KRATE_NATIVE_GUI=1); CI runs them under Xvfb.
WebView2 on Windows needs the Evergreen runtime installed; krate native doctor reports it.

macOS and Windows: the CI native job runs the platform GUI tests on both (macOS TestScenario, Windows TestGUIRoundTrip: page load, request body echo, incremental streaming, secure context), TestGUIShell and TestNativeE2EGUI through a real WKWebView and WebView2. Blocking an in-window navigation to another origin has a real-window test on Windows (TestGUIRoundTrip) but none on macOS, where the navigation delegate is covered only by reading the code.

rows.summary: Responses are streamed to the webview as the handler writes them: headers go out first, body chunks are flushed as they come, a handler panic before the first byte becomes a 500, and closing the reader cancels the handler's context. Server-sent streams from host code use the same path.
knownLimits: macOS and Windows: incremental delivery through a real WKWebView and WebView2 is checked by the platform GUI tests (at least 3 reads spread over 100 ms), and the response writers (macOS task writer: panic before the header, cancel when the task stops; Windows: flush, abort, block buffer) have unit tests that run on both. A reader closed by the page cancelling a real request is driven through a real window on Linux only (TestGUIRequestAbort).

rows.area: Native: host calls, streams and signals
rows.summary: The page calls host functions by id over the scheme: unary calls, server streams and signals (a value with change notifications that reconnects with the current value). Calls are cancellable, errors map to stable codes, concurrency is bounded, and permissions gate which SDK ids a page may reach.
knownLimits: The scheme package is pure Go and identical on every OS; its tests run on Linux, macOS and Windows in CI, and TestGUIShell sends calls, streams and signals from a real WKWebView and WebView2 to host code.

rows.summary: Go host code (functions, streams and signals in .go files next to the pages) runs in a child process under krate native dev and krate native build, and is linked into the single executable in a release build. The child restarts after a crash and reconnects subscriptions.
knownLimits: Needs the Go toolchain on the build machine (krate native doctor reports it).

macOS and Windows: the child process lifecycle (TestChildLifecycle) runs on both in CI, TestGUIShell replaces the Go host binary and restarts the child in a real window, and TestNativeReleaseE2EGUI runs a release executable with Go host code. TestNativeReleaseE2EBrowser (the browser variant) runs on Linux only. On Windows a running Go host binary cannot be replaced, so a Go edit under krate native dev reports that.

rows.area: Native: TypeScript host code on QuickJS
rows.summary: TypeScript host code (*.host.ts files and @host functions) is bundled to one script and runs in the embedded QuickJS engine with no external runtime. Stack traces map back to the TypeScript sources, a watchdog stops runaway synchronous code, and the globals follow the published runtime compatibility ledger.
knownLimits: QuickJS is not Node: only the globals in the runtime compatibility ledger exist; code that needs more selects a node, bun or deno host.

macOS and Windows: the embedded QuickJS engine is pure Go and its tests (calls, streams, the compatibility ledger, runaway recursion) run on both in CI. A TypeScript-only release executable is not run there.

rows.area: Native: Node, Bun and Deno host children
rows.summary: TypeScript host code can run as a child process of the shell under Node, Bun or Deno (native.host.runtime, or native.host.islands for single packages). Deno gets permission flags derived from the app's permissions (including its own unix socket, which recent Deno versions treat as network access); a release build compiles the child into an executable (Node SEA, bun build --compile, deno compile).
knownLimits: Linux: Node children run end to end through the real krate-shell (TestHostChildNode, TestNativeHostChildNodeEndToEnd); Bun and Deno children are covered by the hostchild call tests. Node and Bun release builds are verified; the Deno release command line (deno compile with plain --allow-net for unix targets) is not tested, and the Bun and Node compile tests skip when the tool is missing.
Deno must be recent enough to take unix:<path> in --allow-net (verified with 2.9.8); older versions reject the entry, and the dev command line is not adapted to them.

macOS: Node children run in CI (TestHostChildNode, TestNativeHostChildNodeEndToEnd and the hostchild tests on macos-latest) over a Unix socket. Bun and Deno children are not run through the real shell there.

Windows: Node, Bun and Deno cannot use AF_UNIX there, so the shell uses loopback TCP with a random token. The transport tests (TestTCPHandshake, TestGuardEmptyTokenRejects) and the hostchild tests run on windows-latest, and TestHostChildNode starts a Node child there. Bun and Deno children are not run through the real shell there.
arm64: Bun and Deno publish no Windows on ARM builds, so the windows-11-arm CI job skips those two (KRATE_SKIP_RUNTIMES) and runs Node only; Linux arm64 and macOS run all three.

rows.area: Native: SDK data areas (kv, db, fs, net, os)
rows.summary: The key-value store, SQLite database, scoped file access, HTTP client with secrets, and OS information, directories, secrets and openExternal are available to the page and to Go and TypeScript host code, each behind its permission. Two processes can share a database and a store.
knownLimits: Linux secrets use the freedesktop Secret Service over D-Bus (verified against a fake service); without a provider os.secret answers unsupported.

macOS and Windows: the key-value store, SQLite, scoped files, HTTP client and OS information tests run on both in CI. os.secret (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows) and os.openExternal have no test on either: only the Linux Secret Service is exercised.

rows.summary: Extra windows on routes, title and size, fullscreen, maximize, minimize, frameless windows, close-requested interception and per-window permission scopes bound to the webview, not to anything the page sends. A window can hold several webviews (native-views).
knownLimits: Per-window permission scopes are enforced against the native webview a request came from (see native-view-identity). In browser mode the page's own x-krate-window header is the identity, so a script there can name another window's scope.

Wayland: a client cannot place windows or keep them above others, so SetPosition and SetAlwaysOnTop are accepted and ignored there and the capability report says unsupported. The GUI test packages run under weston (GDK_BACKEND=wayland, weston nested on Xvfb) on full CI runs; no test checks the ignored placement. Window position and always-on-top were verified on X11 only.
Fullscreen, maximize and minimize are verified with openbox on Xvfb (KRATE_NATIVE_WM=1), not on a full desktop environment.

macOS and Windows: window creation, title and size, two windows and per-window scopes bound to the webview run in CI (platform GUI tests, TestGUIScopedWindowCannotForgeAWiderScope). Fullscreen, maximize, minimize, frameless windows, window position, always-on-top and close-requested interception have no test on either OS.

rows.area: Native: requests are bound to the webview they came from
rows.summary: The platform layer tags every request on the app scheme with the webview that made it (WebKitGTK webkit_uri_scheme_request_get_web_view, the webView of WKURLSchemeHandler, one WebView2 WebResourceRequested handler per view) and the shell maps that view to its window or view id and permission scope. The x-krate-window header that page script can set is ignored in a native window, so a scoped page cannot claim a wider scope. A request from a webview the shell cannot place gets a scope that allows nothing.
knownLimits: Browser mode (krate native dev --browser) has no native webviews, so the page's x-krate-window header is the identity there and a script can send another window's id; scopes in browser mode only catch mistakes.
A scope limits what a page may ask the host to do; it does not isolate the page. Every window and view shares one origin, so pages of different scopes can read each other's localStorage and cookies.

macOS and Windows: TestGUIScopedWindowCannotForgeAWiderScope (shell) and TestNativeE2EViewsGUI run in CI against a real WKWebView and WebView2 and check that requests are tagged with the window or view they came from and that the page header is ignored. On Windows the identity is the handler object registered for the view, not a pointer comparison of the sender.

rows.summary: A window can hold several webviews laid out as a tree of horizontal and vertical splits with draggable dividers, minimum pane sizes and ratios that can be read back after a drag. Views are added, removed, focused, navigated and given their own permission scope; they report added, navigated, removed and closed events and can post messages to each other. All views share the app's one web process; an extra view costs about what a page costs (about 1 MB of web process memory on the WebKitGTK 2.54 sysroot, about 40 MB with software-GL compositing on the CI runner). Layout arithmetic is pure Go and tested on every OS; the real-window view tests and the native-views example run in CI on Linux, macOS and Windows.
knownLimits: Divider drags on Linux are verified by calling gtk_paned_set_position, which is what the handle does, not by moving a real pointer.

macOS (nested NSSplitView, Auto Layout minimum sizes) and Windows (several WebView2 controllers in one HWND, dividers hit-tested in the window procedure) run TestNativeE2EViewsGUI in the CI native job. Divider drags on those two are not driven with a real pointer, and the Windows splitter hit-testing and DPI scaling have no tests. The WebView2 NavigationCompleted and WindowCloseRequested handler GUIDs are written from memory of WebView2.h; no platform test asserts the navigated or closed view events on Windows or macOS.
On macOS a page's window.close() does not remove a secondary view (no closed event for it); Linux and Windows do.
Release applies to a whole window, not to one view. While a window is released, adding, removing or re-laying out its views fails.
A divider drag fires no event; read the ratios with layout().
Messages are JSON up to 1 MiB, not queued for a page that has not loaded, and carry the sender's view id only when the sender is a page.

rows.area: Native: print, PDF, find, zoom and capture of a view
rows.summary: Per view (a window's primary view or any added view): the system print dialog, PDF output with page size, margins, orientation and backgrounds, find in page with match counts and stepping, a zoom factor with the Ctrl or Cmd plus, minus and 0 keys kept working, and a PNG capture of the view. WebKitGTK uses GtkPrintOperation, WebKitFindController, the zoom level and webkit_web_view_get_snapshot; WKWebView printOperationWithPrintInfo, findString:withConfiguration:, pageZoom and takeSnapshot; WebView2 ShowPrintUI, PrintToPdf, put_ZoomFactor and CapturePreview.
knownLimits: The print dialog test on Linux closes the GTK dialog programmatically; macOS and Windows open it only with KRATE_NATIVE_PRINT_DIALOG=1 because a test cannot close a system dialog.
The PDF page size and orientation are asserted on Linux only. macOS and Windows tests check for a PDF.

WebKitGTK reports the match count but not the highlighted index (Krate follows it as you step); WKWebView reports only found or not, and WebView2 has no find interface in the WebView2.h Krate builds against, so macOS counts in the visible text and Windows runs window.find and counts the same way.
WebView2 PrintToPdf takes portrait paper dimensions with an orientation, as GTK does; that reading of the settings is untested on Windows.
macOS and Windows: untested. The code is written against the platform APIs, builds for both, and the same GUI tests run in CI on macos-latest and windows-latest.

rows.area: Native: downloads started by the page
rows.summary: Downloads from a link with the download attribute, a blob URL or an attachment response get a destination (the native save dialog by default, or a configured folder with free file names), report started, progress, completed, cancelled and failed events with the final path, and can be cancelled. WebKitGTK uses the download signals, WKWebView WKDownload and WebView2 DownloadStarting. WebKit cannot download the app's custom scheme, so those downloads are fetched from the app handler by the shell and report the same events.
knownLimits: A download of a page of the app origin is requested once more than the page made it, and the file name comes from the link's download attribute only when the link is in the DOM at the time.
Downloads need the downloads area to be linked (the app imports @krate/app/downloads); otherwise the engine's default applies, and downloads of the app's own scheme do nothing.
Windows hands the app origin to WebView2's own download path, which has not been run.

rows.summary: List, get, set and delete cookies by URL, and clear cookies, the cache and storage. WebKitGTK uses WebKitCookieManager and WebKitWebsiteDataManager (cookies persist in the app data directory), WKWebView WKHTTPCookieStore and WKWebsiteDataStore, WebView2 ICoreWebView2CookieManager and ClearBrowsingData.
knownLimits: WebKit keeps no cookies for the app's custom scheme (document.cookie is inert on krate://app and the jar refuses a single-label host such as app), so on Linux and macOS cookie calls for the app origin answer unsupported; pass the URL of an http(s) site. On Windows the app origin is https://app.localhost and has cookies.
An older WebView2 runtime without ICoreWebView2Profile2 can only clear cookies.

Windows on ARM: ClearBrowsingData never finished clearing DOM storage on the windows-11-arm runner's WebView2 and left the webview unusable, so on arm64 the app origin's DOM storage (local storage, IndexedDB, cache storage, service workers, file systems) is cleared through the DevTools protocol (Storage.clearDataForOrigin) instead; storage of other origins in the profile is not cleared there.

rows.area: Native: remote views cannot reach the app
rows.summary: Remote content (web pages) lives in views and windows created as remote (@krate/app/remote). A remote view has its own web context, configuration or profile with no handler for the app scheme and no bridge, so fetches, iframes, images, window.open and navigations to the app fail; the shell gives requests from a remote view the empty scope; navigation is limited to the start origin plus an allowlist, with everything else opened in the system browser or dropped; permissions are denied and downloads cancelled.
knownLimits: Windows resolves https://app.localhost to the loopback address, so that host is refused as a remote URL, allowed origin and navigation target.

Subframes follow the allowlist but never open the system browser. On WebKitGTK the policy callback does not tell main frames from frames, so a refused frame navigation of a remote page is reported with the same verdict as a top-level one.
Opening needs a WebView2 runtime with ICoreWebView2Environment10 (profiles) on Windows.
macOS and Windows: untested. The same GUI tests (gui_remote_test.go) run in CI on macos-latest and windows-latest.

rows.summary: Remote content gets its own storage partition: the default one (persistent, never the app's), named persistent ones (persist:name) and in-memory ones (name). Cookies, local storage, caches, logins and certificate decisions are not shared between partitions or with the app, and a partition can be cleared on its own.
knownLimits: WebKitGTK in-memory partitions use a temporary directory removed at exit rather than WebKit's ephemeral managers, whose certificate exceptions leak between partitions.
macOS before 14 has no named persistent data stores: persist:name answers unsupported and the default partition is in-memory.
Windows clears a profile through an open view of it.

rows.area: Native: request rules for remote views
rows.summary: Declarative request rules per partition (block, redirect, add headers, with URL match patterns) and a request stream, with capability reporting. WebKitGTK blocks with a user content filter and rewrites main-frame navigations; WKWebView with a content rule list and navigation decisions; WebView2 with WebResourceRequested on the remote view.
knownLimits: WebKitGTK and WKWebView cannot redirect or add headers to subresources, and WKWebView does not observe them; capabilities() reports the level per feature.
Block rules on WebKit follow the content-blocker regular expression subset.
macOS and Windows: untested. The same GUI tests (gui_remote_test.go) run in CI on macos-latest and windows-latest.

rows.area: Native: remote user agent, proxy, certificates and logins
rows.summary: A user agent per partition or view, a proxy per partition (WebKitGTK, macOS 14), certificate errors that end the load unless the app accepts the host for that partition, HTTP basic and digest logins answered by the app, and client certificates from PEM files (Linux).
knownLimits: Windows has no per-partition proxy (WebView2 takes --proxy-server for the whole environment) and no client certificates from files; macOS has no client certificates (they need a keychain identity). Those calls answer unsupported.
macOS reports every certificate error as untrusted.
macOS and Windows: untested. The same GUI tests (gui_remote_test.go) run in CI on macos-latest and windows-latest.

rows.summary: The app and a remote page talk only through an opt-in channel: the page calls krateRemote.postMessage, the app gets the engine-reported origin; the app posts to a target origin and the page receives a message event with the app's origin. Messages carry a per-view token, so a frame that never ran the view's script cannot forge one.

rows.area: Native: shared web process, release and background mode
rows.summary: All windows of an app, and all webviews of a window, share one web process (related web views on Linux, one WebView2 environment on Windows). A window can release its webview (hide with release) and get it back on the same route and scroll position; native.window.keepAlive keeps a tray app running with no window; hidden and minimized pages get a krate:memory-pressure event.
knownLimits: macOS and Windows: the pure-Go parts (view state, park on close, quit when empty) run in CI, and one web process per app is not asserted on either OS. No test releases and restores a webview on macOS or Windows, and none tests keepAlive or the memory-pressure event there; the Linux GUI tests are the only run. On macOS the single-web-process switch is a private WebKit selector guarded by respondsToSelector; on Windows ICoreWebView2_19 memory targets need a recent runtime and are skipped without it.
A hidden page that is not released keeps its web process memory; only the page's own handlers of krate:memory-pressure and the shell's heap trim run. Release is what returns the web process memory.
The network process of WebKitGTK stays alive while the app runs, so a released Linux app still holds it.
Release destroys every webview of a window and restores them all with their routes and layout ratios; there is no per-view release.

rows.area: Native: lean pages and the dev Memory panel
rows.summary: Native builds ship no script on a page without client code and do not preload lazy chunks; krate native check and native builds warn (KR7270 to KR7274) about oversized images, large inlined data: URLs, web fonts, compositing CSS effects and long lists without windowing; krate native dev has a Memory panel with PSS, private dirty, DOM nodes and the JS heap where the engine exposes it.
knownLimits: The checks are static: sizes set from CSS classes, values chosen at run time and data fetched later are not seen. The web font check is a heuristic.
WebKit has no JS heap size API, so the Memory panel shows the heap as unavailable on Linux and macOS and points at the web process row.

macOS and Windows: the checks are build-time and platform independent (their tests run on both in CI). Per-process numbers on macOS and Windows come from the memory report of the full CI runs, which is informational (see native-budgets).

rows.area: Native: SDK dialogs, clipboard and menus
rows.summary: Open, save, folder and message dialogs, clipboard text, PNG image and file list, and the menu bar and context menus with click events delivered to Go and to the page.
knownLimits: A native dialog cannot be clicked headlessly: the tests check that it is created with the right options and answer it programmatically.
Windows menu accelerators are shown but not active; Windows message boxes do not support custom button labels.
macOS and Windows: untested. No test creates a native dialog, reads or writes the clipboard or builds a menu there.

rows.summary: clipboard.write puts text, HTML and RTF on the clipboard together; readHtml, readRtf, formats, readFormat and writeFormat read and write by MIME name (UTIs on macOS, registered formats with the CF_HTML header on Windows).
knownLimits: HTML is stored as given on Linux, without a charset declaration.

rows.summary: native.window.contextMenu and menu.setContextMenu disable, replace (custom: event with kind, link, image, selection, spelling; answered with menu items) or extend the engine's context menu per app, window or view; built-in krate: actions for editing, spelling and Inspect Element.
knownLimits: Spelling suggestions and Add to Dictionary are not exercised by any test: no spelling dictionary is available to the Linux test environment.
macOS and Windows: untested; the context menu has a real-window test on Linux only (TestGUIContextMenuCustom). Windows suggestions and Add to Dictionary are best effort.
Inspect Element from a custom menu opens the inspector without selecting the element on WebKitGTK.

rows.area: Native: debugging in krate native dev
rows.summary: krate native dev --debug-go builds the Go host with -N -l and runs it under a headless Delve; breakpoints in src/lib/*.go hit and a Go edit restarts it on the same address. --debug-host starts node, bun and deno host children with --inspect. --debug-config vscode writes attach configurations.
knownLimits: Needs dlv installed; the integration tests skip without it unless KRATE_REQUIRE_E2E is set.
A debugger has to attach again after a Go edit; breakpoints are not carried over.
Windows: untested (the child-wrapping test skips on the CI runner); the Delve integration tests pass on macOS and Windows in CI.

rows.summary: Desktop notifications with actions. On Linux they use org.freedesktop.Notifications over D-Bus; on macOS UNUserNotificationCenter; on Windows, WinRT toasts.
knownLimits: Verified against a real dunst daemon on a private session bus (text, icon, urgency, replacement by id, close from the app and from the daemon with the NotificationClosed reason, default action and action buttons, expiry, daemon gone) and against a fake service for protocol edge cases. Other daemons (GNOME Shell, KDE Plasma) were not run. Without a service that owns org.freedesktop.Notifications the call returns ErrUnsupported.

macOS: no CI test sends a notification there; the bundle planning and the UNUserNotificationCenter path are covered by reading the code. That a notification banner appears and that clicking it or its actions reaches the app are manual checks. It needs an app bundle with a bundle identifier; krate native dev runs the shell from a generated <appId>.dev bundle under .krate/dev. The first notification asks for permission and a refusal is a permission_denied error. Icon and Timeout are ignored, and critical urgency is only time-sensitive (the critical level needs an Apple entitlement).

Windows: no CI test shows a toast; the toast activation URI is tested (TestURIRoundTrip). Clicking a toast and seeing the banner are manual checks. An unpackaged app registers its AppUserModelID under HKCU; a packaged app uses its package identity.

Windows: a toast click uses protocol activation with a per-app URL scheme (HKCU registration for an unpackaged app, NSIS and MSIX registration too), not a COM activator. With the app running, the new process hands the click to it (WM_COPYDATA); with no instance, the click is kept and delivered when the page subscribes (the event that started the app). Unit tests cover the URL, the payload, the registry values and the manifest; the Windows CI job relaunches the test binary with the URL to prove both paths and checks the registration (first run pending), but a real click on a real toast, Action Center after a reboot and the packaged (MSIX) path are not confirmed. Windows has no per-toast timeout or urgency levels, and Show succeeding does not prove a banner was drawn (Focus assist and per-app settings can suppress it).

rows.area: Native: camera, microphone, screen capture and location permissions
rows.summary: The page's getUserMedia, getDisplayMedia and geolocation requests go to the SDK instead of the engine's own policy. A request is denied when its window or view scope lacks media or location; otherwise a remembered decision, the request stream (onRequest in TypeScript, media.OnRequest in Go), the native.media policy (allow, deny or a native prompt) and the operating system's consent decide. Decisions are remembered per app (stored) and per view. The UI half is @krate/app/media.
knownLimits: Linux: verified in a real WebKitGTK 2.54 with the mock capture devices (KRATE_NATIVE_MOCK_CAPTURE): a camera or microphone request reaches the handler with the right kinds and view, allow yields a stream, deny yields NotAllowedError, no handler denies, geolocation deny is PERMISSION_DENIED, and a getDisplayMedia request arrives as kind screen. Real cameras and microphones were not used; no CI runner has one. An allowed geolocation request fails with POSITION_UNAVAILABLE without GeoClue, which the tests accept.

macOS: implemented as a WKUIDelegate (media capture on macOS 12+, a private method for display capture, geolocation where WebKit calls it) and run in CI on macos-latest. A runner has no camera, so the test calls the delegate methods of the real web view with its own blocks. Notification and clipboard requests have no public delegate.

Windows: implemented with PermissionRequested under a deferral and ScreenCaptureStarting (ICoreWebView2_27, absent from older runtimes, which leaves screen capture ungated), with SavesInProfile off so the runtime never answers from its profile. Run in CI on windows-latest; the test runs Chromium's fake devices. getUserMedia with audio and video raises two requests there.
Pointer lock, website data access and the other WebKitGTK request types, and the sensor, download, file and MIDI kinds of WebView2, are left to the engine.

rows.area: Native: media permissions derived from the UI, usage descriptions and capabilities
rows.summary: The build scans the built UI for getUserMedia, getDisplayMedia and navigator.geolocation and grants media and location in a derived build (reported as KR7210 against native.permissions), and in dev for an app without a permission list. Packaging writes the macOS usage descriptions and device entitlements and the MSIX device capabilities from what the UI uses, and the build reports KR7290 when a macOS usage description is missing.
knownLimits: The scan is textual: a call whose API name is built at run time is not found, and a library that mentions getUserMedia asks for the permission. The Info.plist, entitlements and MSIX output are unit-tested as text; no signed macOS app or MSIX package was run.

rows.area: Native: operating system consent for camera, microphone, screen and location
rows.summary: An allowed request is checked against the operating system: AVCaptureDevice, CGPreflightScreenCaptureAccess and CLLocationManager on macOS, the capability consent store on Windows (read only), and the Camera portal under Flatpak or Snap on Linux. media.osStatus reads the state and media.osRequest shows the system prompt where one exists. A refusal denies the request.
knownLimits: Linux: outside a sandbox there is no consent switch for the camera or microphone, and the screen and location go through the ScreenCast portal and GeoClue inside WebKitGTK; only the Camera portal is driven by the SDK, and only against a fake portal in the tests.

macOS: screen recording reads as granted or not yet granted, and a grant takes effect after a restart. Windows: an unpackaged app cannot be shown a consent prompt, so osRequest only reports the state. Both run in CI on their OS, reading the state; no consent prompt is answered there.

rows.area: Native: screen and window capture sources
rows.summary: media.sources lists capturable screens and windows with PNG thumbnails on macOS (CoreGraphics) and Windows (EnumDisplayMonitors, EnumWindows, GDI). No engine accepts a source chosen by the app, so media.chooseSource returns unsupported everywhere and getDisplayMedia always shows the system picker; the SDK can only allow or deny the capture request.
knownLimits: Linux has no list (media.sources returns unsupported, so the row is partial): WebKitGTK reaches the screen through the ScreenCast portal and PipeWire, whose picker is the only list. ScreenCaptureKit is not used on macOS. Window titles and thumbnails on macOS need the Screen Recording permission. The listing runs in CI on macOS and Windows.

rows.area: Native: SDK tray and global shortcuts
rows.summary: A tray icon with a menu (StatusNotifierItem and dbusmenu on Linux with a legacy XEmbed tray fallback, NSStatusItem on macOS, Shell_NotifyIconW on Windows) and global keyboard shortcuts (XGrabKey or the portal on Linux, Carbon RegisterEventHotKey on macOS, RegisterHotKey on Windows).
knownLimits: The tray uses the StatusNotifierItem protocol when a StatusNotifier host exists and falls back to the legacy XEmbed system tray (GtkStatusIcon) when only an XEmbed tray manager owns _NET_SYSTEM_TRAY_S<screen> (X11 only). Stock GNOME with neither returns ErrUnsupported with a hint to install the AppIndicator extension. Verified against stalonetray (XEmbed, with real clicks and menu selection through XTEST) and against the Ayatana application indicator service as a real StatusNotifierWatcher and host; KDE Plasma, GNOME Shell with the extension and other panels were not run.

Linux shortcuts are verified on X11 (XGrabKey, TestGUIGlobalShortcut). On Wayland they need the org.freedesktop.portal.GlobalShortcuts portal, which no test exercises, and return ErrUnsupported without it. No portal backend that implements GlobalShortcuts can run headless here: the GNOME backend needs a running gnome-shell/mutter session, the KDE backend needs KGlobalAccel in a Plasma session, the Hyprland and COSMIC backends are not packaged for Debian or Ubuntu, and xdg-desktop-portal-wlr does not implement the interface.

macOS: TestTrayItemAndMenu runs in CI on macos-latest (a real NSStatusItem with its menu). Carbon hot keys have no test there. Clicking the real status item and pressing a real hot key are manual checks (platform/darwin/MANUAL_TEST.md). With a tray menu any click opens the menu and is reported as click; right-click and double-click are only reported without a menu. Radio items show a checkmark. Single-tone gray icons become template images.

macOS shortcuts use Carbon RegisterEventHotKey (no Accessibility permission). Keys are ANSI key positions, so other layouts differ, and macOS 15 ignores hot keys whose only modifiers are Option and/or Shift. A combination that is already registered is an error. Pressing a real hot key and clicking the real status item are manual checks (platform/darwin/MANUAL_TEST.md).

Windows: on windows-latest TestGUITrayLifecycle adds, modifies and removes a tray icon (it skips when the runner desktop has no taskbar). Hotkey registration and the TaskbarCreated recovery after an explorer restart have no tests. The icon's appearance, its menu behavior, a real explorer.exe restart and real key presses are manual checks. An elevated app is allowed to receive TaskbarCreated with ChangeWindowMessageFilterEx.

Windows: a shortcut another app or Windows holds fails with an 'already registered by another app' error; many Win+ combinations are reserved by the system. The tray menu has no accelerators and one icon per app.

rows.summary: Single instance, deep links and the Linux .desktop entry that registers the app's URL schemes.
knownLimits: URL scheme registration is a packaging step on macOS (Info.plist) and Windows (registry); the runtime code is shared.

macOS and Windows: single-instance locking, stale socket replacement and URL extraction from arguments run in CI on both. No test registers a scheme with the OS or opens a deep link there; the Linux .desktop entry has a test only on its own platform.

rows.summary: native.fileAssociations is validated (extensions, media types, roles, icons) and packaged as macOS CFBundleDocumentTypes with exported UTIs, MSIX file type associations, NSIS ProgID and OpenWithProgids registry entries removed again on uninstall, and a Linux MimeType with a shared-mime-info file in the deb, rpm and AppImage.
knownLimits: Only the generated files are checked: no package was installed on a desktop, so Launch Services, the Windows registry and update-mime-database never read them. The NSIS script was not compiled with makensis and the MSIX was not installed.
An installed app is not made the default handler of a type another program owns, and the viewer role has no Windows equivalent.

macOS and Windows: untested. The same Go code is built for them (cross-compile checks in CI) and the CI native job runs go test on both, but no result of a run against a real WKWebView or WebView2 window has been confirmed.

rows.summary: Files on the command line of the first launch, handed over by a second launch through the single-instance lock, or sent by macOS to the app delegate reach app.onOpenFile and openedFiles (page and Go) with absolute paths, raise the window, and are granted to the fs scope like a dialog pick.
knownLimits: On Linux a first launch with a file and a second launch handing over another were run through the real shell and a real webview (TestNativeE2EFilesGUI); no desktop environment launched the app from a double click.
macOS: the delegate method is called by the test, not by Launch Services. Windows and Linux file-manager launches were not tried.

rows.summary: Files dropped from the desktop onto a view are reported with absolute paths (window.onFileDrop, Go window.OnFileDrop) and granted to the fs scope, while the page keeps its HTML5 drop events: GTK drag signals on Linux, a WKWebView subclass reading the dragging pasteboard on macOS, postMessageWithAdditionalObjects and ICoreWebView2File on Windows.
knownLimits: Linux: a real drag between two GTK windows with synthesized pointer events (xdotool, needs a window manager) delivers the path and the page's drop event. In that setup WebKitGTK offers no File objects to the page with or without the watcher, so File contents were not checked. Without xdotool the real drag test skips; the signal-level tests use plain GTK widgets.
macOS: the drop path is checked with a fake NSDraggingInfo and the class registration; a real Finder drag was not tried.

Windows: the injected script runs against the real WebView2 with a script-made File (which has no path); the COM walk that reads paths is tested with Go fakes of the WebView2.h layouts. A drag from Explorer was not tried and needs a WebView2 Runtime with ICoreWebView2WebMessageReceivedEventArgs2.
Windows: untested. The synthetic drop test skips on the windows-latest runner, so no drop into a real WebView2 window has been confirmed; macOS runs the drop tests against a real WKWebView in CI.

rows.area: Native: release as a single executable
rows.summary: krate native build --release links the shell, the UI, the host code and only the SDK areas the app uses into one executable per target (CGO_ENABLED=0, stripped, with a report of linked and left-out areas). Cross-compiling to the other OSes is covered; an executable built on its own OS runs in the CI native job on macOS and Windows.
knownLimits: TestNativeReleaseE2EGUI builds a release executable on macos-latest and windows-latest and drives it in a real window, and the release tests that need no window run there too. Cross-compiling to another OS is checked for the executable format only; such an executable is never launched.
Needs Go on the build machine; without it (native.release.compile auto) the build falls back to the prebuilt-shell layout.

rows.area: Native: prebuilt shell for apps without Go
rows.summary: The @krate/core-<platform> packages carry krate-shell next to krate. krate native build then writes a runnable dist-native/<os>-<arch>/<productName> with app/ beside it for a TypeScript-only app, with no Go toolchain, and krate native package turns that into tar.gz, deb and the other formats. The shell is found in order: --shell, $KRATE_SHELL, next to the krate executable, a build from a Krate checkout.
knownLimits: The Linux test uses a stand-in shell executable placed next to a copy of the test krate binary and a PATH with no go command; it proves the layout and packaging, not a launch.

The packages for all seven platforms are built by scripts/build-platform-packages.mjs and checked by pnpm check:release; the npm install of them (scripts/smoke-install.mjs) runs in the release workflow.

Alpine (musl): the @krate/core-linux-x64-musl shell is linked with musl's loader (/lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1) instead of glibc's, so it starts and `krate-shell --doctor` runs; the install smoke test checks this on node:alpine in CI. A window needs WebKitGTK 4.1 from the distribution, which was not run on Alpine.

macOS and Windows: the lookup order, layout and packaging tests run in CI on both with a stand-in shell, and the install smoke test installs the @krate/core-<platform> package on macos-latest and windows-latest and runs its krate-shell --doctor. A dist-native build with the prebuilt shell is not launched there.

rows.summary: Reports the Go toolchain, the shell binary and its path, the system webview (WebKitGTK 4.1 version and library paths and display on Linux, the OS version on macOS, the WebView2 runtime version on Windows, through krate-shell --doctor), the packaging and signing tools, and the host runtime the config selects. Exits 1 when something the config needs is missing.
knownLimits: The report logic is tested with injected probes (TestHealthyTypeScriptOnlyLinuxWithoutGo, TestGoRequiredForGoHostAndCompileAlways). The install smoke test runs krate-shell --doctor from the installed platform package on macos-latest and windows-latest. No test checks what the macOS and Windows probes report for a missing or too old webview.

rows.area: Native: krate native test and the app driver
rows.summary: krate native test builds the app like native dev, bundles the project's *.native.test.ts files with esbuild and runs them with node --test. The @krate/app/driver module launches the real shell (--dev) per test file with isolated data directories and drives pages over the dev control channel: evaluate, click, fill, press, text, waitFor, url, errors, calls of host functions and SDK ids, several windows and views, and injected tray, menu and shortcut events for app logic behind native events. Input is DOM-level; real operating-system input is out of scope.
knownLimits: Clicks, typing and key presses are synthesized DOM events (isTrusted is false); native dialogs, the real tray icon, menu bars and notifications cannot be operated, only their events injected.
page.screenshot() is not available: the platform layer has no webview capture API yet.
No --browser mode for tests; they drive the native shell.

The macOS and Windows runs happen only in the CI native job (a desktop session is needed); the per-OS data-directory isolation (HOME on macOS, APPDATA and LOCALAPPDATA on Windows) has not been tried by hand.

rows.area: Native: migration guides and the worked Electron port
rows.summary: Migration guides from Electron and from Tauri v2 map concepts, APIs, security, packaging, updates, testing and debugging to Krate Native. examples/native-from-electron is a small Electron app (electron/, pinned, not run by CI) and its port: host functions and a host signal for ipcMain and webContents.send, an application menu, a tray, dialogs, scoped file reads and writes, a notification, a kv settings store and a second window. krate native test drives the port through the real shell.
knownLimits: The Electron original is a reference and is not built or run in CI.

Native dialogs and notification banners cannot be clicked headlessly: the test calls the code behind the dialogs and accepts 'sent' or 'unsupported' for the notification and tray (Linux without a notification service or tray host answers unsupported).
The macOS and Windows runs happen only in the CI native job.

rows.summary: A plugin is a Go package plus a krate-plugin.json (name, Go import path, permissions with descriptions, ops, minimum Krate). native.plugins enables local directories, npm packages and Go modules; ops are callable as plugin/<name>.<op> (lowerCamel op names like the SDK ids, bound to Go names by capitalizing or an explicit go field) with generated codecs and a typed krate/plugin/<name> TypeScript module (calls, streams, signals). Plugins run inside the shell process with a context (lifecycle hooks, Dispatch, platform capabilities, data directory), cannot register ids outside their namespace, and their permissions (plugin:<name>.<permission>) are derived from the code, enforced per window, listed by krate native check and shaken per op in release builds. An app with plugins runs under a per-app shell built with go (cached by plugin set, sources and Krate version) in dev and in builds; krate native plugin init scaffolds one.
knownLimits: The plugin runtime and the build are exercised on all three OSes: TestNativePluginGUI builds a per-app shell and checks a granted call in a real window (the full CI runs add -run Plugin on macos-latest and windows-latest), TestNativePluginAllowlist checks the allowlist, and the shell and plugin package tests check namespaces and the permission gate. The system-info example's own tests run on all three on full runs; its macOS CPU load (ps) and Windows (GetSystemTimes) readings are checked for shape, not for accuracy.
Plugins are trusted Go code in the shell process; the namespace and permissions limit what a page can reach through them, not what the plugin does.
Plugin ops are callable from pages; TypeScript host code reaches them only by id (__krateHost.call). A go: plugin needs network or a populated module cache for the first build.
Editing a local plugin's Go code restarts native dev instead of hot-reloading it.

rows.summary: krate native package builds .tar.gz, .deb, .rpm and AppImage on Linux, .app, .zip and .dmg on macOS, and .zip, NSIS installer and MSIX on Windows, from a release executable or the prebuilt-shell layout, with icons, desktop entries and update files. The Windows installer checks for the WebView2 Runtime and, by native.bundle.windows.webview2, downloads or embeds Microsoft's bootstrapper or ships a Fixed Version runtime folder; the app shows a message box with the download link when the runtime is missing.
knownLimits: On Linux the .deb, .rpm and AppImage of examples/native-tasks are built, and the .deb contents and AppImage were launched and checked to serve the first page (scripts/native-smoke.mjs; the CI native job installs the .deb with dpkg and runs the AppImage). The .rpm is checked for structure and not installed.

macOS: the CI native job builds the .app, .zip and .dmg of examples/native-tasks, verifies and mounts the .dmg, copies the app out, checks its signature (ad hoc) and launches it (version, first page, window open for 8 seconds). Windows: it builds the .zip, the NSIS installer and the MSIX, runs the NSIS installer silently (registry entry, launch, uninstall) and installs the MSIX with Add-AppxPackage, signed with a test certificate. Dragging the .dmg to Applications, the installer UI and Start menu entries are manual checks; the NSIS installer needs makensis.

arm64 packages are built for linux/arm64, windows/arm64 and darwin/arm64 (deb and rpm architecture, MSIX ProcessorArchitecture, AppImage ARCH, Windows resources) and checked by unit tests; the CI native job also runs on ubuntu-24.04-arm and windows-11-arm, where the packaging steps run natively. Those two jobs have not run yet, and makensis, the Windows SDK and appimagetool may be missing on the Windows on ARM image (each is skipped with a notice, not failed).

WebView2: the registry check and the stand-in bootstrapper run are exercised by a full-run CI step (scripts/native-smoke.mjs windows webview2); the message box shown when the runtime is missing has no test. The Fixed Version runtime loader path uses the runtime type value from open reimplementations of the loader and is not confirmed. An MSIX cannot declare the Evergreen runtime as a dependency (it is not a framework package), so an MSIX app relies on the runtime being present (Windows 11, current Edge) and on the message box.

rows.summary: krate native sign and notarize drive codesign and notarytool on macOS, signtool or osslsigncode for Windows, and gpg for Linux packages, and rebuild the archives around the signed payload. CI signs for real with throwaway keys (gpg on Linux, a self-signed identity in a temporary keychain and an ad hoc signature on macOS, a self-signed code-signing certificate on Windows) and verifies with gpg --verify, codesign --verify --deep --strict, signtool verify /pa and Get-AuthenticodeSignature.
knownLimits: Unit tests replace the signing tools with stand-ins (command lines, ordering and secret redaction). The CI native job also signs for real with throwaway certificates (scripts/native-smoke.mjs): macOS ad hoc and with a self-signed identity in a temporary keychain (codesign --verify --deep --strict), Windows with a self-signed Authenticode certificate (signtool verify /pa), Linux packages with a generated gpg key (gpg --verify, and a tampered copy must fail). Ad hoc signing and the Windows test certificate ran green on macos-latest and windows-latest; the temporary-keychain identity, signtool verify /pa and the gpg step are new and their first CI run is pending.

Notarization needs an Apple Developer account and stays manual, as do Developer ID identities, certificates from a CA (EV or OV Authenticode), timestamps from a paid authority and hardware or cloud signing services.

rows.summary: krate native build --release --arch universal compiles darwin/arm64 and darwin/amd64 and package merges them in pure Go into one .app: the executable and every shared Mach-O file (Go host child, compiled Bun and Deno hosts, Node single executables) become fat binaries with FAT_MAGIC, one fat_arch per slice and 2^14 alignment. The update target is darwin-universal (zip, latest-darwin-universal.json), which the running app learns from a krate-dist.json marker. The Linux and Windows columns mean the merge runs there (a cross build from any OS).
knownLimits: The fat Mach-O is written by Krate and read back with debug/macho (TestPackageUniversalMacApp). Running both slices (native, and x86_64 under Rosetta) and lipo -info are checked by the universal app packaging step of the full CI runs on macos-latest only.

A Node host needs a node binary per architecture (KRATE_NODE_DARWIN_ARM64 / KRATE_NODE_DARWIN_AMD64); Bun and Deno cross-compile by themselves. The prebuilt-shell layout holds one platform, so a universal app needs the compiled-executable layout.

rows.summary: krate native package --format flatpak writes a flatpak-builder manifest on org.gnome.Platform (WebKitGTK 4.1) with finish-args derived from the app's permissions, a desktop file, AppStream metainfo (validated with appstreamcli when installed), icons named by the app id and a Flathub manifest that builds from a source archive with a sha256. With flatpak-builder installed it builds a .flatpak bundle. Inside the sandbox the shell opens links and sends notifications through the portals, uses the file chooser portal (GTK_USE_PORTAL), names its tray item below its own id and keeps data in the sandbox XDG directories.
knownLimits: The manifest, metainfo and portal calls are tested without Flatpak (command lines, files, a fake D-Bus). Building the bundle and running the app inside a real sandbox needs flatpak-builder and the GNOME runtime and has not been done; the first CI run of that step is pending. appstreamcli validation of the generated metainfo has not run on any machine yet.
Flathub prefers apps built from source; a prebuilt-binary submission is reviewed case by case, and screenshots must be added to the metainfo by hand.

rows.summary: krate native package --format snap writes snap/snapcraft.yaml (core24, gnome extension, libwebkit2gtk-4.1-0 staged, plugs derived from the app's permissions) with the app and icon, and builds the .snap with snapcraft when it is installed. Inside a snap the shell uses the OpenURI and notification portals, GTK_USE_PORTAL and the snap's XDG directories, and has no self-updater.
knownLimits: The snapcraft.yaml is checked as text; building it with snapcraft and running the snap under strict confinement has not been done. The exact plugs a WebKitGTK app needs under strict confinement (for example for the tray) are unconfirmed.

rows.summary: krate native package --target mas builds a sandboxed .app: com.apple.security.app-sandbox with network.client, user-selected files, camera, microphone and location entitlements derived from the app, inherit-only entitlements for helper executables, the embedded provisioning profile (checked against TEAMID.appId), codesign with a 3rd Party Mac Developer Application or Apple Distribution identity (ad hoc without one) and a productbuild .pkg signed with the installer identity. native.updater is removed and the running sandboxed app refuses updater calls.
knownLimits: The entitlements, Info.plist, tool command lines and failure cases are unit tested on any OS. TestNativeMASSandboxGUI signs the example ad hoc with the sandbox entitlement and runs its GUI flows inside the container on macOS; it passes in CI on macos-latest. Uploading to App Store Connect, a real distribution identity and App Store validation have not been tried.
Access to a file the user picked lasts for that run; security-scoped bookmarks are not used.

rows.summary: krate native package --format msix-store builds the Store variant of the MSIX with the Partner Center identity (name, publisher id, publisher display name), no self-updater and a static check of the full-trust rules, plus a .msixupload; --arch universal --target windows/amd64 bundles x64 and arm64 into an .msixbundle (AppxBundleManifest.xml, block map, uncompressed packages) and its .msixupload. The Linux and macOS columns mean the package is built and checked there.
knownLimits: The bundle manifest offsets are consistent with the zip layout (tested), but neither makeappx nor the Windows App Certification Kit nor Partner Center has opened a package; the Windows column stays untested until a runner does (makeappx unbundle, Add-AppxPackage of a signed copy).

rows.summary: In-app updates: an Ed25519-signed feed, resumable verified downloads, signed delta updates (pure Go bsdiff patches for the install tree, macOS bundle and AppImage, with fallback to the full file), staged rollouts with halt/critical/min_version, channels, and an apply step that replaces the executable and app directory (Linux, AppImage, macOS bundle, Windows ordering) with rollback on failure and rollback of a version that fails its first start.
knownLimits: The macOS bundle and Windows apply, delta and rollback steps are file-system logic tested on Linux (the delta and rollback tests run the macOS bundle and Windows wrapper layouts with GOOS overridden); replacing a running Windows executable has not been tried on Windows. scripts/native-smoke.mjs runs, for each OS, a real update 1.0.0 to 1.1.0 of an installed packaged app (TestSmokeUpdateInstalledApp, which must now be a delta), a confirmed healthy start, and a 1.1.0 build whose host exits early being rolled back on its second launch (TestSmokeRollbackState). The full update passed in the CI native job on Linux, macOS and Windows before deltas and rollback were added; the delta and rollback flows have run on Linux only so far.

First-start protection does not see a crash before the shell's start-up check runs (a loader error, a panic in a package init), and the first update from a version built without it is not protected. An installer-based install (NSIS, MSIX, deb, rpm) does not take delta updates or rollbacks: the updater replaces an install directory, a bundle or an AppImage.

rows.area: Native: app icon badge and progress
rows.summary: krate/badge.* sets a badge (count or short text), a progress value (none, normal, indeterminate, error, paused) and an urgent flag on the app icon. Linux emits the Unity LauncherEntry D-Bus signal that GNOME Dash to Dock, KDE and Plank read; macOS uses NSDockTile with a progress bar in the tile; Windows uses ITaskbarList3 progress and an overlay icon the SDK draws.
knownLimits: Linux launchers show numbers only (other text is refused as unsupported) and no indeterminate state; the signal was verified with a listener on a private D-Bus session, not in a real dock.
macOS draws error and paused as normal progress.
macOS and Windows: the same Go code is built for them; TestNativeE2ESystemGUI calls the badge API there and accepts a working call or an unsupported answer, so what the OS shows is not checked.

rows.summary: krate/screen.* lists displays (bounds, work area, scale, primary, refresh rate), finds the display of a window, centers a window on a display and reports display changes. GDK monitors on Linux, NSScreen on macOS, EnumDisplayMonitors and GetDpiForMonitor on Windows.
knownLimits: Linux was run against Xvfb, which has one monitor; multi-monitor layouts are covered by the pure geometry tests, not a real second monitor.
Display change events are wired to GDK monitors-changed, NSApplicationDidChangeScreenParametersNotification and WM_DISPLAYCHANGE; no test drives a display change.

rows.area: Native: power, idle and sleep blockers
rows.summary: krate/power.* reports on-battery, idle time and lock state, delivers suspend, resume, lock, unlock, battery, AC, idle and active events, and holds sleep blockers. Linux uses logind, UPower, Mutter IdleMonitor or the ScreenSaver service, and the GNOME session manager or PowerManagement inhibitors; macOS NSWorkspace, IOKit and IOPMAssertion; Windows WM_POWERBROADCAST, WTS session notifications and SetThreadExecutionState.
knownLimits: Linux was tested against fake services on private buses, never a real suspend or lock.
logind's Inhibit returns a file descriptor, which the SDK's D-Bus client cannot receive, so it is not used.
Battery and idle events come from sampling every three seconds while an event stream is open.
macOS: untested (only the event tracker is tested there). Windows runs the GUI power test in CI. A real suspend was never tried on any OS.

rows.summary: krate/login.get and set register the app to start at login: an XDG autostart entry on Linux, SMAppService with a LaunchAgent fallback on macOS, the HKCU Run key on Windows.
knownLimits: A packaged (MSIX) Windows app declares a startupTask extension instead; the calls answer unsupported because toggling a StartupTask from code is not implemented.
macOS: SMAppService needs a signed bundle and was never run; the LaunchAgent fallback writes the plist but does not call launchctl, so it takes effect at the next login.
